html:
The ruins of Ostia, the port town of ancient Rome at the mouth of the Tiber, 25 km southwest of the city; its name comes from the Latin os, "mouth". Legend makes it Rome's first colony, founded by the fourth king, Ancus Marcius, but the oldest remains found are of the 4th century BCE, and the oldest standing building is the 3rd-century fort at its core. It served as a naval base in the First Punic War and grew into the port where Rome's imported grain came in. Marius sacked it in 87 BCE, and pirates burned the port in 68 BCE, a shock that led Rome to give Pompey his command against them. Walls were begun in 63 BCE, under Cicero as consul.

Under the emperors Ostia ran the grain supply for the grain dole, and when Claudius and Trajan built the great harbour of Portus nearby, the trade made it rich: by the 2nd century it had about 50,000 people, and Hadrian rebuilt much of it. Its streets show how ordinary Romans lived: apartment blocks of several floors with shops on the ground floor, warehouses for grain, a theatre built under Agrippa, a forum with a temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, many baths, inns and a fire brigade. Eighteen shrines of Mithras have been found here, and the remains of the oldest synagogue yet known in Europe, probably built in the late 1st century.

Trade moved to Portus after Constantine made it a separate town, but Ostia lived on as a seaside town for the rich, with baths still working in the 5th century. Augustine's mother Monica died here in 387. As Rome shrank after 476 the town decayed, and after a sea battle with Saracen raiders in 849 its last people moved away. Sand dunes covered it, and the sea now lies 3 km off because the river silted the coast. Only Pompeii and Herculaneum are better preserved. Large digs under Mussolini in 1939 to 1942 opened much of the site, yet about two thirds of the town is still unexcavated.
